title: The Left-Handed Universe
subtitle: Winter 1956: a physicist cancels the trip of a lifetime, freezes a speck of cobalt to a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, and finds out that the mirror lies.
crosslink: Like true science told as a story? More true science stories →
intention: you'll tell the true story of the experiment that broke one of physics' oldest assumptions, and use the language of cause and effect — due to, thereby, which meant that, resulting in, so that — to explain how something works and why it matters.
warmup: Hold your right hand up to a mirror. The reflection is a left hand. Is there anything in the laws of nature that would notice the difference — or is the mirror world just as possible as ours?
Think of something 'everybody knew' that turned out to be wrong. What was the moment it fell — and who paid the price for being right?
If you design an experiment and someone else has the idea, who deserves the prize?
vocab_intro: Before we read, let's unlock the words you'll need — half of them physics, half of them the language of proving people wrong. Think first; the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A. Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: A snowflake has symmetry: rotate it a sixth of a turn, or reflect it in a mirror, and it looks exactly the same.
items.meaning: symmetry (n) — the property of staying the same under a change such as rotation or reflection. (adj: symmetrical)

items.sent: Physicists say a quantity is conserved when the total never changes: energy is conserved — it can move around, but none is created or lost.
items.meaning: conserved (adj) / conservation (n) — in physics, kept constant through every process. A conservation law.

items.sent: Cobalt-60 is unstable: over years its nuclei decay, each one turning into nickel and spitting out an electron.
items.meaning: to decay (v) / decay (n) — of an atomic nucleus, to break down spontaneously into something else, giving off radiation.

items.sent: She was meticulous: every wire checked twice, every temperature logged, nothing left to chance or to an assistant.
items.meaning: meticulous (adj) — extremely careful and precise about every detail.

vocab.heading: B. From the meaning to the word
vocab.instruction: Which word fits the definition? The first letter is given. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: A proposed explanation that has not yet been tested — the thing an experiment is designed to confirm or destroy. It begins with h.
items.meaning: a hypothesis (n) — a testable proposed explanation. Plural: hypotheses. (v: to hypothesise)

items.sent: To arrange things so that they all point the same way — atoms in a magnetic field, for instance. It begins with a.
items.meaning: to align (v) — to line up in the same direction. (n: alignment)

items.sent: To prove wrong and replace something that was accepted — a ruling, a theory, a record. It begins with o.
items.meaning: to overturn (v) — to reverse or abolish something established. The experiment overturned a law.

vocab.heading: C. Choose the meaning
vocab.instruction: One sentence, three options. Say a, b or c — then reveal.

items.sent: Every particle has a property called spin, which behaves like a tiny rotation with a definite direction. Spin here is: (a) a kind of speed (b) an intrinsic property of a particle that behaves like rotation (c) the temperature of a nucleus
items.meaning: (b) — spin (n) — a fundamental property of particles that behaves like rotation about an axis and gives them a direction.

items.sent: Most senior physicists greeted the idea with scepticism; one of them bet money it was wrong. Scepticism is: (a) enthusiasm (b) fear (c) doubt; an unwillingness to believe without proof
items.meaning: (c) — scepticism (n) — a doubting attitude that demands evidence. (adj: sceptical)

items.sent: The prize went to the two men who had asked the question, and the woman who answered it did not get the credit. Credit here is: (a) money lent by a bank (b) public recognition for having done something (c) a university course
items.meaning: (b) — credit (n) — recognition or praise for an achievement. to get / take / deserve the credit for something

vocab_use: Sort the ten words into the physics and the people. Which words could belong to both?
Using hypothesis, overturn and credit, predict what happens in this story — and who ends up famous.
story_intro: A true story, told here in three parts. Everything in it happened — the dates, the temperatures, the bet. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

story.title: Part 1 — The question nobody wanted to ask
paras: In 1956 physics had a small, ugly problem called the theta–tau puzzle. Two particles had been found that were identical in every measurable way — same mass, same lifetime — except that one decayed into two pions and the other into three. Under the rules, that should have been impossible: the two decays had opposite 'parity', and parity, everyone knew, was conserved. Parity is mirror symmetry. It says that the laws of nature cannot tell left from right: film any experiment, project the film in a mirror, and what you see is also a possible experiment. It had been assumed for so long that nobody thought of it as an assumption. It was just how the universe was.

Two young theorists at Columbia University and the Institute for Advanced Study, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, did something unusual that summer. Instead of inventing a clever explanation to save the rule, they asked whether the rule had ever been tested. They went through the literature. For gravity, for electromagnetism, for the strong force that holds nuclei together, the evidence for mirror symmetry was overwhelming. For the weak force — the force responsible for radioactive beta decay — there was none. Nobody had ever checked. In October they published a paper suggesting that parity might simply not be conserved in weak interactions, and proposing experiments that could decide it.

The reaction was not excitement. Wolfgang Pauli, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, wrote to a colleague that he could not believe God was a weak left-hander, and offered to bet a large sum that the experiments would find nothing. Richard Feynman took a bet at fifty to one against. Most physicists thought the question was barely worth asking: the idea that the universe might secretly prefer one hand over the other seemed not so much wrong as absurd. The experiments Lee and Yang had proposed were also fiendishly difficult, which was a good excuse for not doing them.

One person did not think it absurd. Chien-Shiung Wu, a professor at Columbia, was the most exacting experimenter in beta decay alive. Born near Shanghai in 1912, she had come to America in 1936 to study, had worked on the Manhattan Project, and had spent a decade cleaning up other people's careless measurements of exactly the kind of decay Lee and Yang were talking about. Lee had come to her for advice before the paper was written. When she read it, she understood at once that there was a way to do the test — and that if she did not do it immediately, somebody else would.

check.q: What is parity, and what exactly did Lee and Yang discover when they searched the literature?
check.a: Parity is mirror symmetry — the assumption that the laws of physics are the same in a mirror-reflected world. Lee and Yang found that it had been tested thoroughly for gravity, electromagnetism and the strong force, but never once for the weak force responsible for beta decay.

check.q: How did the physics establishment react, and who took the idea seriously?
check.a: With scepticism bordering on ridicule: Pauli said he could not believe God was a 'weak left-hander' and offered to bet on it; Feynman bet fifty to one against. Chien-Shiung Wu, Columbia's leading beta-decay experimenter, saw immediately how the test could be done.

story.discuss: Lee and Yang's breakthrough was not an answer but a question: 'has anyone actually checked?' Why is that question so rarely asked — and why did it take two outsiders in their twenties and thirties to ask it?

story.title: Part 2 — A hundredth of a degree
paras: The experiment Wu designed sounds simple and was anything but. Take cobalt-60, a radioactive nucleus that decays by emitting an electron. Each nucleus has a spin, a built-in direction like a tiny arrow. Line up all the arrows so they point the same way, then count the electrons: how many fly out along the direction of the spin, and how many against it? In a mirror-symmetric universe, the two numbers must be equal, because a mirror turns one direction into the other and the laws cannot know the difference. If more electrons came out one way than the other, the universe was, in a precise sense, left-handed.

The difficulty was the lining up. Nuclei are jostled by heat; at any ordinary temperature their spins point every which way. To align them you need a powerful magnetic field and a temperature so low that thermal motion almost stops — about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero. Only a handful of laboratories in the world could reach it. One of them was the National Bureau of Standards in Washington, where Ernest Ambler and a small team had mastered a technique called adiabatic demagnetisation, which cools a crystal by switching off the field that had been holding its atoms in order. Wu needed their refrigerator, their crystal and their patience; they needed her cobalt, her detectors and her certainty about what a clean result would look like.

There was a cost. Wu and her husband, the physicist Luke Yuan, had booked passage on the Queen Elizabeth for a long-planned journey to Asia — the first time either had been back in twenty years. Wu cancelled. Her husband went alone. Through the autumn she shuttled between New York and Washington, teaching at Columbia during the week and living in the Washington laboratory at weekends, and the team fought a series of exhausting technical battles: the cobalt had to sit on the surface of the cooling crystal in a layer thin enough not to warm it, the detectors had to work inside the cryostat, and every time the apparatus warmed by a fraction of a degree the alignment was lost and the count had to begin again.

In the days before Christmas 1956 the first counts came in. The electrons were not symmetric. Far more of them were flying out against the direction of the nuclear spin than along it. Wu telephoned Lee and Yang, but she refused to announce anything. Being meticulous, she assumed the effect was an error in her own apparatus until it had been proven otherwise, and spent two more weeks trying to destroy her own result — reversing the field, checking the thermometry, ruling out every alternative she could imagine. It survived everything. By early January the team was certain. The asymmetry was enormous, not a subtle statistical whisper but a shout: the mirror image of their experiment was one that could not happen in this universe.

check.q: Explain the design of Wu's experiment in your own words — what was measured, and what result would break parity?
check.a: Cobalt-60 nuclei were aligned in a magnetic field at about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, and the electrons from their decay were counted along and against the spin direction. Mirror symmetry demands equal numbers; an unequal count means the weak force can tell left from right.

check.q: What did Wu give up to do it, and what did she do when the first results appeared?
check.a: A long-planned voyage to Asia with her husband — she cancelled and he went alone. When the counts showed a huge asymmetry she refused to announce it and spent two weeks trying to prove her own result wrong before accepting it.

story.discuss: Wu spent two weeks attacking her own discovery before she would believe it. Is that the most important thing a scientist does? What is the equivalent in other kinds of work?

story.title: Part 3 — Who gets the credit
paras: Word travelled fast. At Columbia, Leon Lederman heard of Wu's preliminary result over lunch in early January and, with two colleagues, redesigned an experiment on decaying muons that was already running; within days they had an independent confirmation. On 15 January 1957 Columbia held a press conference — a rare thing in physics then — and the New York Times put the story on its front page: a basic concept of physics had been overthrown. Pauli, who had been so sure, wrote that he was glad he had not actually placed the bet, because he could have afforded to lose some reputation but not the money. Feynman paid up.

The consequences went far beyond a puzzle about two particles. If the weak force distinguishes left from right, then the universe is not indifferent to handedness after all; the neutrino, it turned out, comes in only one form, always spinning one way relative to its motion, like a screw that only turns anticlockwise. Within a year physicists had found that other cherished symmetries were also broken by the weak force, and the search for what is and is not conserved became one of the central themes of the century, leading eventually to the questions of why the universe contains matter and not antimatter. All of it began with the assumption that nobody had thought to test, and the woman who tested it.

In the autumn of 1957 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Lee and Yang, for the question. It was not awarded to Wu, for the answer. The reasons have been argued about ever since: the prize's reluctance to honour experimenters who confirm a theory; the number of people on her team; the fact that Lederman's group had published almost simultaneously; and, many have concluded, the fact that she was a woman and an immigrant in a profession that gave its prizes to men. Wu never campaigned. She said in later years that she was hurt by it, and went on working. She became the first woman to be president of the American Physical Society; she received the inaugural Wolf Prize in 1978, an award created partly to recognise those the Nobel had passed over; students called her the First Lady of Physics, and a generation of experimenters learned from her that a result is not a result until you have failed to break it.
She died in 1997. The cobalt experiment is still taught in every university physics course in the world, usually under a name that gives the credit correctly at last: the Wu experiment.

check.q: How was the result confirmed and announced, and what did it lead to?
check.a: Lederman's Columbia group confirmed it within days using muon decay; Columbia announced both on 15 January 1957 and the New York Times put it on the front page. It revealed a universe that distinguishes left from right, led to the discovery that other symmetries are broken by the weak force, and opened the question of matter versus antimatter.

check.q: Who received the 1957 Nobel Prize, and what recognition did Wu eventually receive?
check.a: Lee and Yang, for proposing the question; Wu was left out. She later became the first woman president of the American Physical Society and received the first Wolf Prize in 1978; the experiment is now taught everywhere as 'the Wu experiment'.

story.discuss: The prize went for the question, not the answer. Lee and Yang asked something nobody dared to ask; Wu did what nobody could do. If you had to give one prize, who gets it — and what does your answer say about what you think science is?

grammar.h2: The grammar this story runs on: cause and effect
grammar.intro: To explain physics — or anything — you have to connect a cause to its effect precisely: what makes what happen, and how surely. Vague connectors ('and then', 'so') make an explanation sound like a story. These make it sound like an argument.
notes:
1. Giving the cause.
• because of / due to / owing to + noun: "The spins point every way due to thermal motion."
• as / since + clause (the reason is already known): "Since nobody had tested it, the assumption survived."
• result from / stem from / arise from: "The asymmetry results from the weak force."

2. Giving the effect.
• lead to / result in / give rise to / bring about + noun: "Cooling the crystal leads to alignment."
• thereby + -ing (formal — the effect of the action just described): "They switched off the field, thereby cooling the crystal."
• which meant (that) / which is why: "The count fell to zero, which meant that the alignment had been lost."

3. Purpose and condition.
• so that / in order that + clause; so as to / in order to + verb: "She cooled the sample so that the nuclei would align."
• If… then for logical consequence: "If parity is conserved, then the two counts must be equal."
The stronger your verb — results in rather than leads to — the more certain you sound. Choose deliberately.

exercises.h3: Cause or effect? Choose the connector
exercises.instruction: One each, from: due to · thereby · which meant that · so that · results in. The grammar after the gap tells you which fits.
items: The nuclei were cooled to a hundredth of a degree ___ their spins would line up in the field.
At room temperature the spins point in every direction ___ thermal motion.
Reversing the magnetic field reverses the spin direction, ___ testing whether the electrons follow it.
More electrons flew out against the spin than along it, ___ the mirror image of the experiment was impossible.
Any warming of the apparatus ___ the loss of alignment.

exercises.instruction: Join each pair into one precise sentence using the connector in brackets. Say it, then reveal.
items: Nobody had tested parity in weak interactions. The assumption survived for decades. (since)
The team switched off the magnetic field. The crystal cooled. (thereby)
Wu cancelled her voyage. The experiment could start in the autumn. (so that)
The electron count was asymmetric. Parity was not conserved. (which meant that)
Lederman's group published at the same time. Wu's contribution was harder to isolate. (as a result of)
answers: Since nobody had tested parity in weak interactions, the assumption survived for decades.
The team switched off the magnetic field, thereby cooling the crystal.
Wu cancelled her voyage so that the experiment could start in the autumn.
The electron count was asymmetric, which meant that parity was not conserved.
As a result of Lederman's group publishing at the same time, Wu's contribution was harder to isolate.

exercises.h3: Put it together — explain the experiment in one paragraph
exercises.instruction: Fill each gap with the connector the hint asks for. Then read it aloud as if teaching it.
items: Cobalt-60 decays by emitting an electron; ___ (since) each nucleus has a spin, the electrons can be counted along and against it. ___ (if… then) parity is conserved, ___ the two counts must be equal. Wu cooled the sample to 0.01 K ___ (so that) the spins would align, and reversed the field ___ (thereby) checking that the electrons followed the spin. Far more electrons emerged against the spin than along it, ___ (which meant that) the weak force distinguishes left from right — a result that ___ (led to) the collapse of one of physics' oldest assumptions.
answers: since · If … then · so that · thereby · which meant that · led to

grammar.outro: In the Speak tab you'll explain the experiment to someone who has never heard of it — and the connectors will do most of the work.

deeper.h2: Why this story stays with you
paras: Physics likes to present itself as a machine for finding truth, and this is one of the cases where the machine worked: a puzzle, a brave question, a decisive experiment, a front page, a prize, a new picture of the world, all inside eighteen months. But the story also shows the machine's parts. Pauli and Feynman — two of the greatest minds of the century — were sure enough to bet, and were wrong, not because they were foolish but because an assumption that has never been tested feels exactly like a fact. Lee and Yang's genius was to notice a feeling and call it an assumption.

And then there is the question of credit. The Nobel committee has rules, and the rules favoured the theorists; the omission of Wu was, on paper, explicable. It was also part of a pattern — Lise Meitner, Rosalind Franklin, Jocelyn Bell Burnell — of women whose experiments and observations made other people's prizes possible. Wu's own answer was not a campaign but a standard: the two weeks she spent trying to destroy her own result are the reason the result stood. Whatever the committee decided, the universe was left-handed, and she was the one who had found out.
deeper.note: Look again at the mirror. Before 1957, if you had been shown a film of any physical process and its mirror image, you could not have said which was the real world. After Wu, you can: watch a cobalt nucleus decay and see which way the electrons go. The mirror world is not merely different — it is impossible. What does it mean that the universe has a handedness at all?
questions: 'An assumption that has never been tested feels exactly like a fact.' What untested assumptions do you suspect in your own subjects — or your own life?
Wu cancelled a journey she had waited twenty years for, because if she waited, someone else would do the experiment. Was that ambition, duty or fear? Would you have gone on the ship?
Lee and Yang got the prize for asking; Wu did the answering. Which is harder? Which is rarer? Why does the world usually reward the first?
The Wolf Prize was created partly to recognise people the Nobel had missed. Is a second prize a correction, or an admission that the first one cannot be fixed?

speak.useful: Explaining: "Because of…", "…which meant that…", "…thereby…", "…so that…", "If…, then…". Weighing credit: "It was X who…", "Without…, … would never have…", "You could argue that…". Hedging a claim: "It appears that…", "The evidence suggests…".

tasks.label: Task A · Teach the experiment (4 minutes)
paras: Explain the Wu experiment to someone who has never heard of parity — what was assumed, what was measured, why the temperature mattered, and what the result meant. Move through: the mirror → the theta–tau puzzle → 'has anyone checked?' → cobalt-60 and spin → a hundredth of a degree → the asymmetry → the front page.
Use cause-and-effect connectors in nearly every sentence, and at least five key words (symmetry, conserved, decay, meticulous, hypothesis, align, overturn, spin, scepticism, credit).

tasks.label: Task B · The Nobel committee (4 minutes)
paras: It is October 1957 and you are on the committee. Make the case for giving the prize to Lee and Yang alone — the rules, the theory, the simultaneous confirmation. Then make the case, for one minute, that Wu must share it, and say what you would actually have done.

tasks.label: Task C · A test nobody ran (4 minutes)
paras: Tell the story of a belief that lasted because nobody tested it — in science, in history, in sport, in daily life — and what happened when someone finally did. Use cause and effect to explain both why it survived and how it fell.
menu: Heavy objects fall faster than light ones — until someone dropped two balls.
The four-minute mile was thought to be physically impossible until 1954.
Stomach ulcers were caused by stress, until a doctor drank a beaker of bacteria to prove otherwise.
A 'rule' at your school or in your family that everyone obeyed and nobody could explain.
The idea that continents cannot move.
A 'fact' about food, sleep or exercise that you grew up with and later found was never true.

final: Feynman lost a bet on this and laughed about it. Pauli was relieved he had not placed his. What does it cost a great scientist to be wrong in public — and should it cost anything?
Wu said the result hurt her, and went on working. Is that admirable, or should she have fought? What would fighting have looked like in 1957?
If the universe can tell left from right, is it stranger, or more beautiful, than a perfectly symmetrical one?
Before you go — from memory: explain in three sentences why the two electron counts had to be equal if parity was conserved — one sentence with if… then, one with so that, one with which meant that.
